geology-oil-formation: Oil begins as microscopic marine life — plankton and algae — that sinks to the seabed and gets buried under layers of mud. Heat and pressure over millions of years 'cook' the organic matter in a process called maturation, turning it first into kerogen, then into liquid oil and gas. The classic recipe needs temperatures between about 60 and 120°C, and most of the world's oil formed in warm, productive seas.
geology-oil-reservoirs: An oil reservoir is a porous rock layer that holds oil like a sponge — usually sandstone or fractured limestone. Porosity gives the rock space to store oil; permeability lets it flow toward a well. The oil sits in tiny spaces between grains, often with gas above and water below. Geologists map reservoirs with seismic surveys and well data, then estimate how much oil can actually be recovered.
geology-oil-traps: Oil migrates upward through rock until something stops it — a trap. Structural traps are folds or faults that bend impermeable layers over the oil; stratigraphic traps form where a porous layer pinches out or is sealed by a change in rock type. The classic anticline dome, an upward arch capped by shale, holds most of the world's giant fields. Finding traps is the heart of petroleum exploration.
geology-drilling: Drilling for oil is engineering in the dark: a rotating bit on a kilometre-long pipe grinds through rock while drilling mud circulates down and back up, cooling the bit and carrying rock chips to the surface. Sensors on the bit report rock type, pressure, and gas in real time. A modern well can reach 10 kilometres deep — the world's deepest, the Kola borehole, passed 12 kilometres but was drilled for science, not oil.
geology-fracking: Hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, unlocks oil and gas trapped in shale by creating cracks: fluid is pumped into a well at high pressure, splitting the rock along natural weaknesses, then sand props the fractures open so gas can flow out. Combined with horizontal drilling, fracking turned the United States into a top producer within a decade. The method stirs debate over water use, induced earthquakes, and chemical additives — all subjects of intense geological research.
geology-natural-gas: Natural gas is mostly methane, formed alongside oil or on its own where organic matter cooked at higher temperatures. It is the cleanest-burning fossil fuel, emitting about half the carbon of coal, which is why it often replaces coal in power plants. Gas accumulates in the same traps as oil but needs an impermeable seal — being lighter, it escapes more easily. It is also the main source of helium.
geology-coal-geology: Coal is fossilized swamp: layer after layer of plant matter buried in oxygen-poor water, compressed and heated over millions of years. Peat becomes lignite, then bituminous coal, then hard anthracite as depth and pressure increase — each step raising carbon content and energy density. Coal seams record ancient tropical forests, and some contain whole fossilized trees. The great coal deposits of the Carboniferous, about 300 million years ago, powered the Industrial Revolution.
geology-uranium-geology: Uranium concentrates in a few deposit types: sandstone roll-front deposits, where groundwater carried uranium until chemistry dropped it out; and vein or unconformity deposits in ancient basement rock. Canada's Athabasca Basin holds some of the world's richest ores, grading hundreds of times higher than average rock. Mining uranium usually means in-situ leaching — dissolving it underground and pumping the solution out. Uranium's decay, not its chemistry, is what makes it so valuable.
geology-geothermal-geology: Geothermal energy taps the heat of Earth's interior, which grows hotter with depth — about 25 to 30°C per kilometre. Where magma or hot rock sits close to the surface, water circulates through fractures and returns as steam or hot water. Iceland generates a quarter of its electricity from geothermal fields, and many countries use the heat directly for buildings and greenhouses. Deep geothermal systems can work almost anywhere, but drilling that deep is expensive.
geology-carbon-storage: Geological carbon storage captures CO₂ from power plants or industry and injects it deep underground into porous rock — the same sandstones and saline aquifers that held oil and gas for millions of years. A caprock of shale keeps the gas trapped, and the CO₂ slowly dissolves and mineralizes into solid carbonate. Norway's Sleipner field has stored over 20 million tonnes under the North Sea.
geology-lithium: Lithium, the lightest metal, is the core of modern batteries, and its geology comes in three flavours: hard-rock spodumene deposits in pegmatites (Australia's main source), lithium-rich clays, and brines in high-altitude salt flats like the Salar de Atacama, where the sun evaporates water and concentrates lithium. Brines are cheap but water-hungry; hard rock is energy-intensive to refine. Demand is exploding for EVs, and geologists are racing to map every economically viable deposit.
geology-cobalt: Cobalt rarely forms its own deposits — most is a by-product of copper and nickel mining, especially in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which supplies over half the world's output. It concentrates in sediment-hosted copper belts and in nickel laterites, where tropical weathering enriches the ore. Cobalt gives lithium-ion batteries their stability and longevity, making it a critical mineral for the green transition. Its supply chain's social and environmental costs drive research into alternatives.
geology-oil-sands: Oil sands are a mix of heavy, tar-like bitumen, sand, clay, and water, found mainly in Alberta and Venezuela. Unlike conventional oil, bitumen is too thick to pump, so it is mined in giant open pits or softened underground with steam before extraction. Producing it takes more energy and water than conventional oil, raising its carbon footprint — but the deposits are among the largest on Earth.
geology-shale-gas: Shale gas is natural gas trapped inside fine-grained, organic-rich shale, rock so impermeable that gas cannot flow until it is fractured. The shale itself is both the source rock and the reservoir — the gas formed where it sits. Horizontal wells now drill along the shale layer for kilometres, and fracking releases the gas. Major plays like the Marcellus and Barnett shales transformed energy markets. Shale holds more natural gas than all conventional fields combined.
geology-petroleum-system: A petroleum system is the complete recipe for oil and gas: a rich source rock, enough heat to cook it, a path for it to migrate, a porous reservoir, and an impermeable seal with a trap. Miss any ingredient and there is no field. Geologists map all five elements across a basin to predict where oil might hide — the 'fairway' where every condition overlaps. The system concept turned petroleum geology from luck into science.
geology-peak-oil: Peak oil is the moment when global oil production reaches its maximum and begins an irreversible decline. The idea dates to geologist M. King Hubbert, who correctly predicted US production would peak around 1970. Debate continues over when the global peak arrives — estimates range from 'already past' to decades away, depending on demand and technology. The deeper truth: oil is finite, easy oil is depleting, and each new barrel costs more energy to find.
geology-energy-transition-geology: The shift from fossil fuels to clean energy is, at heart, a mining problem: wind turbines, solar panels, batteries, and grids need enormous quantities of copper, lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths, and steel. A single EV uses about six times more minerals than a conventional car. Meeting climate goals could require a several-fold increase in mineral production by 2040.
geology-oil-history: Oil has been used for thousands of years — ancient Mesopotamians waterproofed boats with bitumen — but the modern industry began in 1859 when Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial well in Pennsylvania. Kerosene replaced whale oil for lamps; then the automobile made gasoline king. Oil shaped the twentieth century: wars, economies, and geopolitics revolve around its fields.
geology-geologic-hazards-energy: Energy development can wake up the ground. Wastewater injection from oil and gas operations has triggered small earthquakes in Oklahoma and Texas, and geothermal plants occasionally induce microseismicity. Coal mining causes subsidence and mine fires that can burn for decades. Hydroelectric reservoirs add weight that can stress faults. Understanding these induced hazards is now a routine part of energy geology — monitoring instruments watch for trouble before communities feel it.
